subject: biology
topicDisplay: Health, disease and the development of medicine
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Eduqas Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: White blood cells and immune response

questions.q: The World Health Organisation defines good health as:
options: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
Having a strong immune system only
questions.explain: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease. Both communicable and non-communicable diseases affect health.

questions.q: Which of these is a COMMUNICABLE (infectious) disease?
questions.explain: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread between individuals (e.g. flu). Heart disease, diabetes and most cancers are non-communicable - they do not spread.

questions.q: Which is a lifestyle risk factor for a NON-communicable disease?
options: Being coughed on by an infected person
Smoking, which increases the risk of lung cancer
questions.explain: Non-communicable diseases are linked to risk factors such as smoking, poor diet, alcohol and lack of exercise. Smoking greatly increases lung cancer and heart disease risk.

questions.q: How do viruses typically make us feel ill?
options: By reproducing inside body cells and damaging them
questions.explain: Viruses invade cells and reproduce inside them, damaging or destroying the cell when new viruses are released. Bacteria often make us ill by producing toxins.

questions.q: Malaria is caused by a protist spread by which vector?
questions.explain: Malaria is caused by a protist (Plasmodium) spread by the bite of infected mosquitoes, which act as vectors. Control focuses on preventing mosquito bites and breeding.

questions.q: Which type of pathogen causes the fungal plant disease and body infections such as athlete's foot?
questions.explain: Fungi are eukaryotic pathogens that cause diseases such as athlete's foot and rose black spot in plants. They can be single-celled (yeast) or multicellular.

questions.q: Which measure would help REDUCE the spread of a communicable disease?
options: Good hygiene such as handwashing and isolating infected people
questions.explain: Spread is reduced by hygiene (handwashing), isolating infected individuals, destroying vectors, safe food/water and vaccination. These break the transmission route.

questions.q: Which is a PHYSICAL barrier that stops pathogens entering the body?
questions.explain: The skin is a physical barrier. Other non-specific defences include mucus and cilia in the airways (physical) and stomach hydrochloric acid and lysozyme in tears (chemical).

questions.q: How does the stomach help defend against pathogens?
options: It produces hydrochloric acid that kills many pathogens in food
questions.explain: The stomach produces hydrochloric acid, which kills many pathogens swallowed in food and drink - a chemical (non-specific) defence.

questions.lo: White blood cells and immune response
questions.q: One way white blood cells defend the body is by phagocytosis. This means they:
questions.explain: In phagocytosis, white blood cells (phagocytes) engulf and digest pathogens. Other white blood cells (lymphocytes) produce antibodies and antitoxins.

questions.lo: White blood cells and immune response
questions.q: Antibodies produced by lymphocytes are described as SPECIFIC because they:
options: Are the same for all diseases
Have a shape complementary to one particular antigen
questions.explain: Each antibody has a specific shape complementary to a particular antigen on a pathogen. Memory cells allow a faster, larger response if the same pathogen returns.

questions.q: How does a vaccine provide protection against a disease?
options: It contains antibiotics that kill the pathogen
It introduces dead or inactive pathogen (antigens) so the body makes antibodies and memory cells
It provides extra red blood cells
questions.explain: A vaccine contains dead or inactivated pathogens/antigens. These stimulate lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory cells, giving rapid immunity if the real pathogen invades.

questions.q: If a large proportion of a population is vaccinated, the disease struggles to spread. This is known as:
questions.explain: Herd immunity occurs when enough of the population is immune (usually through vaccination) that the pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting even unvaccinated individuals.

questions.q: Why do antibiotics NOT work against viral infections such as the common cold?
options: Viruses live and reproduce inside body cells, which antibiotics cannot target without harming the cell
questions.explain: Antibiotics kill bacteria (e.g. by damaging cell walls). Viruses reproduce inside host cells, so antibiotics cannot reach them without harming our own cells.

questions.q: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria develops because:
options: Resistant bacteria survive treatment and reproduce, passing on resistance
questions.explain: By natural selection, a few bacteria with resistance survive antibiotic treatment and reproduce, so the resistant allele becomes more common. Overuse speeds this up (e.g. MRSA).

questions.q: Which action helps SLOW the development of antibiotic resistance?
options: Stopping antibiotics as soon as you feel better
Only using antibiotics when necessary and completing the full course
questions.explain: Resistance is slowed by not over-prescribing antibiotics, only using them when needed, and completing the full course so all bacteria are killed.

questions.q: New medicines are tested for three main things before use. These are:
options: Toxicity (safety), efficacy (does it work) and dose
questions.explain: New drugs are tested for toxicity (safety), efficacy (whether they work) and the correct dose. Testing goes through preclinical (cells, tissues, animals) then clinical trials.

questions.q: In a clinical trial, a placebo is given so that:
options: The effect of the drug can be compared with no active treatment (control)
The drug is tested on animals
questions.explain: A placebo (dummy treatment) acts as a control so that any real effect of the drug can be distinguished from psychological effects. Double-blind trials reduce bias.

questions.q: (Separate science) Monoclonal antibodies are produced from:
options: Many different white blood cells at random
A single type of cell, cloned to make identical antibodies
questions.explain: Monoclonal antibodies are made from a single clone of cells, so they are all identical and bind to one specific antigen. They are used in pregnancy tests and to target cancer cells.

questions.q: (Separate science) Why are monoclonal antibodies useful in a pregnancy test?
options: They bind specifically to the hormone hCG in urine
questions.explain: Monoclonal antibodies in a pregnancy test bind specifically to the hormone hCG produced in pregnancy, giving a visible result. Their specificity makes them ideal detectors.
